To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a combination of saturation mutagenesis and directed evolution of three active‐site residues of Rhodococcus ADH‐A resulted in an enzyme with an altered enantiopreference and an increased catalytic efficiency with the (R) enantiomer of 1‐ phenylethanol.

the W295A substitution in alcohol dehydrogenases from Rhodococcusspecies fundamentally changes the stereopreference and that the obtained change in enantioselectivities can be explained by a shift of the nonproductive substrate binding mode and a faster NADH release.

the enantio‐selective alcohol dehydrogenases from Rhodococci can be modified by directed evolution to favor a nonpreferred substrate enantiomer, which can be explained by a shift from nonproductive to productive substrate binding and by a faster rate of coenzyme turnover.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an alcohol dehydroghase with improved enantioselectivities, and the results provide new insight into the mechanism of stereoselectivity in this class of enzymes.
the mechanism of enantioselective catalysis by ADH‐A and how this can be manipulated.
the identification of a key residue for enantiopreference in ADH‐A and the elucidation of how the catalytic efficiency with the less‐preferred enantiomer is improved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed increase of the (R) enantiomer preference is due to a combination of effects, including a change in the rate‐limit step of the catalysis, a change in the nonproductive binding modes, and a change in the active‐site structure.
the nonproductive substrate binding in ADH‐A is not the main reason for the enantioselection.
the enantioselection of ADH‐‐A with 1‐phenyl‐ethanol can be attributed to a combination of a nonproductive binding mode and a slower rate of coenzyme dissociation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the observed change in stereoselectivity can be explained by a combination of two mechanisms, namely an altered rate‐limiting reaction step in the catalytic cycle and a shift in substrate binding.

the enantioselection of ADH‐‐A is based on the combination of two mechanisms: a nonproductive substrate‐enzyme interaction and a stereoselective catalytic step, which both are modulated by a single amino acid residue.
a combination of directed evolution and structural analysis has provided a detailed understanding of the molecular mechanism behind enantioselective alcohol dehydrogenases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nonproductive binding mode can be a key factor in determining the enantioselection in ADH‐A, and that it is possible to change the nonproductive binding by targeted protein engineering.

the discrimination between the two enantiomers of 1‐phelylethanol is not only determined by differences in the binding of the preferred (S)‐alcohol but also by differences in the nonproductive binding of the less favored (R)‐enantiomers.
nonproductive substrate binding can contribute to substrate discrimination in ADH‐A and that it is possible to modify the enantiopreference of ADH‐ A by directed evolution.
